title: Agent0-VL: Self-Evolving Vision-Language Agent with Tool-Integrated Reasoning
one_liner: A vision-language model learns to improve itself by using real tools to check its own reasoning and repair its mistakes without any human feedback.
lead: When a vision-language model (a system that reads images and text together) reasons about a hard visual question, it gets stuck because it can only judge itself using words alone. This causes mistakes and false confidence. Agent0-VL fixes this by letting the model use real tools—like math calculators or image analyzers—not just to reason, but to verify its own reasoning and catch its own errors, all without any human supervision.

problem.h2: Vision models judge themselves badly using only words
paras: A large vision-language model (a trained system that reads both images and text) can answer questions about pictures—like reading a chart or solving a spatial puzzle with shapes. But when it answers wrong, it has no way to catch itself. If you ask it to check its own work, it reads its previous answer in words and tries to spot the error, also in words. This fails because:

The model tricks itself. When checking a chart answer, it might invent false numbers or misread the axis without noticing, because it is reasoning only from its own text, not actually looking at the real chart again.

A beginner tries: 'Just have the model re-read its own reasoning.' But that means checking words with words—like checking a spelling test by reading it a second time. You see what you expect to see, not what is really there.
So reasoning stays stuck: the model makes mistakes and falsely judges itself as correct (because re-reading its own text gives no ground truth), which means it never learns to correct its errors.

callout.html: A vision-language model has no way to verify its visual reasoning is actually correct, because it can only use text to judge text.

panels.title: 1. The question arrives
panels.caption: A vision-language model reads a chart and must answer a question about it.

panels.title: 2. It guesses with confidence
panels.caption: The model generates an answer without checking against the real data.

panels.title: 3. Old way: re-read the text
panels.caption: Previous self-checking: read the model's own written answer again to spot errors. This fails.

panels.title: 4. New way: use real tools to verify
panels.caption: Agent0-VL runs a real tool on the image data to check: did that number match the chart?

panels.title: 5. Learns what went wrong
panels.caption: The model sees the gap between its guess and the tool's verdict, and tunes its weights to avoid that error.

steps.text: The model reasons about the image using real tools—a calculator for math, a measurement tool for shapes and distances, a chart-reading tool. It generates a multi-step reasoning trace.
The same model now flips to a second hat: it looks at its reasoning trace and uses tools again to check each step against the real image data.
When the verifier finds a mistake (the guess does not match the tool's measurement), it writes plain feedback: what went wrong and why.
The verifier assigns a score based on whether the reasoning passed the tool-based checks, without needing any human-written labels.
The model learns to predict reasoning traces that will pass tool-based verification. Over time, it gets better because it tunes weights away from patterns tools reject, toward patterns tools confirm.

paras: The paper changes the self-correction target: instead of having the model judge text-against-text, it grounds verification in real tool outputs. A tool gives an objective answer (a measured distance, a correct sum, a pixel coordinate) that the model's reasoning must match.

hidden.h2: Verification correctness: do the tools agree?
hidden.name: Tool-grounded verification accuracy
paras: The paper introduces and measures a hidden quantity: how often the model's reasoning passes verification when checked against real tools. This is not the model's final answer accuracy—it is the meta-accuracy: does the model's self-check (when grounded in tools) correctly identify right and wrong reasoning?

The paper estimates this by having the verifier run tools on the image and compare the reasoning trace to the tool outputs. When tool output and reasoning match, verification passes. When they conflict, verification fails. The model learns the pattern: reasoning that tools will confirm is good reasoning.

heat.caption: Darker means grounded in tools. Light gray means text-only, no verification ground truth.

reads.html: The model learns by seeing whether tools agree with its reasoning. Correct reasoning agrees with tools; incorrect reasoning does not. The model tunes itself to make reasoning that tools will confirm.

Agent0-VL unifies solver and verifier roles; the verifier generates structured feedback by running tools and comparing outputs to reasoning traces, producing self-reward signals without external annotation.

paras: The root cause of bad self-judgment was hallucination: the model re-reading its own text invents false supporting details and never catches itself. Tools break this loop because a tool's output is objective. A calculator does not hallucinate: two plus three is five, every time.

When the verifier runs tools on the actual image (not just re-reading the reasoning text), it gets a ground truth. If reasoning said the average is 42 but the calculator says 38, that gap is real and visible. The model learns: this kind of reasoning pattern led to an error I can actually prove.

Why does this work without human labels? Because tools provide the labels automatically. The tool outputs are the objective ground truth. The model's job shifts: predict reasoning that will make sense when checked by tools. Over time, the model tunes its weights to favor reasoning patterns that tools validate, and suppresses patterns that tools reject.

The self-evolving cycle is stable because it has a concrete anchor: if the model hallucinates in its reasoning, the tool will contradict it. The model cannot convince itself that hallucinated reasoning is correct if a calculator proves otherwise.

stages.s: Solver uses tools to reason (e.g. calculator, chart reader)
Verifier re-runs tools on the reasoning steps
Compare: does reasoning match tool outputs?
Assign reward (correct if match, error if mismatch)
Model learns to prefer reasoning tools will confirm

math.words: The reward for a reasoning trace is the fraction of reasoning steps that pass tool-based verification, multiplied by a weight that grows as training progresses.
symbols: one complete reasoning sequence from question to answer
one step in the reasoning (e.g., read chart value, add numbers)
the objective result from running a tool on the image
1 if reasoning matches tool output, 0 if it conflicts
a growing weight as the model improves (encourages stricter verification)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Reasoning trace: Read chart value as 42, then add 8, get 50.
Tool verification: Chart value is actually 40 (mismatch at step 1). Tool sum is 48 (mismatch at step 2).
Matches: 0 out of 3 steps matched the tools.
Reward = 0/3 * 1.5 = 0.0. Model is penalized; it will adjust.
New trace attempt: Read chart value as 40, add 8, get 48.
Reward = 3/3 * 1.5 = 1.5. Model is reinforced; this pattern gets stronger.

math.note: The model learns to output reasoning that tools will confirm as correct, step by step.

charts.title: Text-only self-evaluation (baseline)
charts.note: Re-reading text does not improve much because the model still invents false supporting details.

charts.title: Agent0-VL (tool-grounded)
charts.note: Tools provide objective ground truth. The model learns that reasoning matching tool outputs gets rewarded.

items.html: If a tool sometimes gives wrong answers (e.g., a chart reader that misdetects pixels), the model learns the tool's errors. The fix: use tools that are reliable, or combine multiple tools to cross-check.

If a reasoning step is vague (e.g., just say the value without showing work), the verifier might struggle to match it to a tool output. The fix: enforce structured reasoning (step by step, not shortcuts).

Chart questions have objective answers (read the axis correctly), but some visual reasoning tasks may require aesthetic judgment or open-ended interpretation. Tools cannot ground those. The paper focuses on tasks with objective ground truth.

On chart reasoning, shape puzzles, and visual science tasks—where an objective answer exists and a tool can verify it—the model reliably improves, because each error produces a concrete tool-based signal showing what went wrong.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple chart-reasoning task: show a bar chart with numerical values. Ask the model to compute statistics (sum, average, maximum). Have Agent0-VL reason through the steps using a calculator tool, then verify each step by having the tool recompute. Let the model fine-tune itself by seeing which reasoning patterns the tool confirms. Over 50 iterations, the model should learn to reason more accurately without any human corrections; measure accuracy before and after.
demo.closing: The demo must show that tool-based self-verification alone (no human labels) teaches the model to reason correctly.
